title: Joy
hookLine: the joy of the Lord is your strength
tomorrow: why is a line from a prison letter printed on gym shirts?

lines: THE CROWD WEEPS AT THE WORDS.
cards: A funeral lunch, and somebody tells the story about Grandpa and the lawn mower, and the whole room laughs through its tears. Can you feast on the same day you cried?

One crowd in the Bible was told to, and that's the odd part. They stand in the street before the water gate in Jerusalem while Ezra the scribe reads the book of the law aloud, from morning until midday. And they weep.
Then their leaders stop them. Not with a sermon on sorrow. With an order to throw a party.

teach.h: WHY STOP THE TEARS? A HOLY DAY.
teach.b: Here's the order, from Nehemiah: “Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
So why stop the tears? The text gives the reason: the day is holy, a feast day. Weeping has its place.
Ecclesiastes says there is “A time to weep, and a time to laugh.” This was the time to laugh. Notice what's built into the party: portions sent to anyone with nothing ready.
Joy here isn't private; nobody is left out of it. Then the strange phrase itself: the joy of the LORD. Readers take it two ways.
Joy in the LORD, the gladness people find in God. Or the LORD's own joy, shared with his people. Either way, the crowd doesn't have to manufacture it.
It's given, and it holds them up. And here's the turn worth telling a friend: the chapter says they went off “to make great mirth, because they had understood the words that were declared unto them.”

teach.h: THE WORDS THAT MADE THEM CRY.
teach.b: The same words that made them cry became the reason to feast.
Some Christians put it this way: happiness rises and falls with what happens; joy can sit underneath it, the way a floor sits under a room.

how: Christians mark joy in worship through singing, shared meals and feast days; some read Nehemiah 8:10 as a reminder that joy in God can hold steady even in hard seasons.

o: a cheerful mood you keep up for others
a deep gladness, given, that holds you up
the feeling of finally getting what you want

games.q: the day of tears and the feast — tap the pairs.

s: Nehemiah tells the weeping crowd to keep mourning
he says “neither be ye sorry”: go eat, drink, and send portions.
the feast included food sent to people with nothing ready
“send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared.”
joy, in Nehemiah 8, means pretending you were never sad
they wept first; then the same words they'd understood became the reason to feast.

games.q: your team loses the final. the coach still takes everyone for pizza, and makes sure the bench kid who never got in gets the first slice. which part of Nehemiah 8 is that?
o: send portions to them for whom nothing is prepared.
neither be ye sorry: act like the loss never happened.
read the law aloud from morning until midday.
games.why: the feast had a rule built in: send portions to anyone with nothing ready. joy shared, so nobody is left out.

practice: Pick one simple good thing within reach: a sip of something warm, a bite of something sweet. Taste it slowly, as if it were the feast, with no phone and no next thing. If you pray, let the enjoying itself be the thanks.

wordCard.voice: Joy. A gladness that is given, not manufactured, and that holds people up, even on a day that began in tears.

orig.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness. the word in 'the joy of the LORD is your strength' (Nehemiah 8:10).

carryVoice: Pocket this one: joy is strength; the crowd in tears went home to feast and share. See you tomorrow.
